title: Kidney Stone
short: Bone loss puts calcium in your urine. One morning it becomes a stone, and then a fever.
briefing: In weightlessness your bones lose calcium and it ends up in your urine, so kidney stones are one of the top medical risks of a long mission. Watch pain, hydration, temperature and heart rate. The water unit, the medical kit and the sleep station can all help.

story.intro: A week after the spacewalk, a quiet morning of lab work. Then a pain in your side that won't let you sit still.
story.goal: Get the pain under control, keep drinking, and catch any sign of infection early.

crew.text: The samples you brought in are already in the freezer. Earth is very excited about tray three.
Bone loss up here puts calcium in your urine. Stones are one of the things I watch for.
Houston has an early return plan ready if we need it. Let's make sure we don't.

carry.goodText: You came back from the spacewalk with margin to spare and drank well afterwards, so you start hydrated.
carry.badText: The spacewalk ran you dry and you never caught up: you start dehydrated, which makes stones worse.

events.text: Day 48. A quiet morning of lab work.
Sudden, cramping pain in your right side and back. It comes in waves.
Chills. Your temperature is starting to climb.
The stone has passed. Dr. Okafor bags it for the lab on Earth.

decisions.title: Pain out of nowhere
decisions.prompt: The pain comes in waves, from your back round to your belly. You can't get comfortable and you feel sick.

choices.label: Call Dr. Okafor and get your kidney scanned
choices.feedback: Waves of side pain you can't lie still through are typical of a kidney stone. Tell the medical officer, then scan with the ultrasound in the medical kit.

choices.label: It's a pulled muscle from the spacewalk. Stretch it out and keep working
choices.feedback: A strained muscle hurts when you move and eases when you keep still. Pain that comes in waves and won't let you settle points to a stone, not a muscle.

choices.label: Wait and see if it goes away before telling anyone
choices.feedback: On a station, the medical officer needs to know early. The ultrasound, the medicines and the ground team all take time to bring in.

decisions.title: Too sick to drink
decisions.prompt: You feel sick and the last thing you want is water.

choices.label: Take the anti-sickness medicine and keep sipping water
choices.feedback: Staying well hydrated keeps your urine dilute, and settling the nausea makes drinking possible. Small steady sips work better than big gulps.

choices.label: Stop drinking until the pain settles
choices.feedback: Drying out concentrates your urine, which is how stones form and grow. Space already pushes extra calcium into it.

choices.label: Drink two litres right now to flush it out
choices.feedback: Forcing down a big volume doesn't push a stone out faster, and it can make you vomit. Steady sips do the job.

decisions.title: Fever and chills
decisions.prompt: You're shivering, your temperature keeps rising, and the pain in your side hasn't gone.

choices.label: Start antibiotics now and tell Mission Control you may need to go home early
choices.feedback: A fever with a blocked kidney can mean infection trapped behind the stone, which is an emergency. Start antibiotics now, and Houston gets an early return ready in case they aren't enough.

choices.label: Take paracetamol for the fever and keep an eye on it
choices.feedback: Paracetamol hides the fever, but the infection keeps growing behind the stone. Treat the cause: antibiotics, and tell the ground.

choices.label: Get in your sleeping bag and sleep it off
choices.feedback: An infected, blocked kidney can lead to sepsis within hours. Never sleep off a fever and shivering when you have a stone.

actions.label: Sip 300 ml of water
actions.message: Small sips, and it stays down.

actions.label: Take ibuprofen
actions.message: An anti-inflammatory is usually the first choice for stone pain. It also eases the swelling around the stone.

actions.label: Ultrasound scan of your kidney
actions.message: Dr. Okafor guides the probe. The scan shows a swollen right kidney and a 5 mm stone low down in the ureter, small enough to pass on its own.

actions.label: Take tamsulosin
actions.message: Dr. Okafor's prescription. It relaxes the tube from the kidney so a stone this size passes more easily.

actions.label: Start antibiotics
actions.message: Antibiotics started. Tell Mission Control too.

actions.label: Rest with a warm pack
actions.message: Warmth on your side takes the edge off the cramps.

keySteps.label: Confirm the stone with the ultrasound
keySteps.why: Other problems can cause pain like this. A scan shows the stone, how big it is, and whether the kidney is blocked.

keySteps.label: Keep drinking through the nausea
keySteps.why: Dilute urine helps a stone pass and stops new ones from forming.

keySteps.label: Start antibiotics when the fever starts
keySteps.why: Infection behind a blocked kidney can become sepsis within hours. Start antibiotics early, then decide about going home.

successText: The stone has passed and the fever is gone. You're back on light duties tomorrow.
failText: The pain and infection got out of control. Mission Control is preparing an early return.
